title: Max turns a mountain into a battery (it ran dry first)

beats.text: Max's mountain battery just ran dry, and his kids are still holding lanterns.
Let's rewind to that sunny afternoon.
His solar panels make spare power. Max wants it saved for tonight's movie.
First, a pond beside the lake. With almost no drop, the turbine barely turns.
Hydropower needs head, a big fall. So Max lifts the reservoir 150 metres.
A skinny, twisting pipe brings it down. Friction chokes it; the bulb flickers.
So he bores a seven-metre pressure tunnel. Roughly 200 cubic metres of water rush through each second.
Lights blaze, until the top runs dry. An ordinary turbine can't send water back up.
Two reversible 125-megawatt pump-turbines fix that. Spare daytime solar spins them backwards, pumping the same water uphill.
As the top drains, the head falls from 175 to 125 metres. The fixed-speed machines shudder.
Variable-speed motor-generators shift between about 285 and 315 rpm, staying efficient all the way down.
Solar pumps it up by day; after sunset, power flows within 90 seconds. Movie on, lanterns off. Real plants: 1,500 megawatt-hours, 250 megawatts for six hours, 80 years. Would you build one?
